burden_scope.value: Customization and integration effort, resource and cost mismatch, toolchain fragmentation, interoperability and semantic-conversion burdens, training and organizational maturity, and lack of measurable return-on-investment evidence.

crd1_objectives.value: The review aims to synthesize space-systems-engineering MBSE practices and best-practice patterns, classify and assess methods, languages, and tools across five phases, and identify implementation challenges and opportunities.

crd2_sources_and_restrictions.value: Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched, supplemented by 24 gray-literature reports from MB4SE collections, ASCEND conferences, and NASA technical documents. Scopus was limited by year, Engineering subject area, English, and excluded keywords; Web of Science used MBSE and space in all fields for 2011–2022. Scopus timing/count is inconsistent (February 2023/191 versus 20 March 2023/192), and no exact Google Scholar or gray-route strategies or dates are supplied.

crd3_eligibility_criteria_and_applicatio.value: Eligible reports, peer-reviewed articles, and conference papers had to present space-mission MBSE applications at any mission size, subsystem, or space-segment level. Exclusions covered pre-2011 work; antenna, embedded-system, and software applications; nonspace aeronautics/defense/naval work; space-science exploration discussions; comparison, experience, overview, and evaluation reports; inaccessible content; and similar/incomplete reports. Metadata screening used title, year, keywords, and exclusions, followed by detailed content review. Screener numbers, independence, and disagreement handling are not reported.

crd4_quality_or_validity_criteria.value: No study-level quality or validity criteria are reported. The report's validity exercise instead asks three external experts to rate samples of the review authors' method, language, and tool classifications and reports kappa agreement.

crd5_appraisal_application_and_use.value: No primary-evidence appraisal is applied or used in synthesis. External classification-agreement feedback was used to resolve classification ambiguity and refine the scheme, not to weight, exclude, stratify, or interpret studies by evidence quality.

crd6_data_extraction.value: Each included item was mapped to one or more of five MBSE phases; method, language, tool, mission/project, and publication descriptors were extracted into Excel and appendix tables. Three external experts checked sampled classifications, but the report does not state who performed extraction, whether it was duplicated, or how extraction discrepancies among authors were handled.

crd7_data_synthesis.value: The authors combine VOSviewer bibliometric keyword analysis, inductive method classification, function/tool-based language and tool classification, descriptive frequency and phase matrices, and qualitative narrative/cross-analysis for phase relationships, challenges, and opportunities. No meta-analysis is performed.

crd8_investigation_of_differences.value: Differences are explored descriptively through mission classes, publication characteristics, method archetypes, language/tool groups, and phase distributions. There is no formal heterogeneity, subgroup-by-evidence-quality, or sensitivity analysis, and the authors caution that report-level phase markings may not represent entire mission implementations.

crd9_data_combination_and_reasonableness.value: Descriptive classification and frequency combination is broadly suitable for heterogeneous space-MBSE literature and no unjustified effect-size pooling is attempted. Its reliability is limited by inferred language coding, ambiguous source terminology, unequal detail, and internally inconsistent flow counts and denominators.

crd10_conclusions_flow_from_evidence.value: Partly. The broad taxonomies, utilization patterns, and phase mappings are traceable to study-level appendix matrices and descriptive figures, and the authors acknowledge major limitations. Claims about best strategies, effectiveness, and lifecycle value are less secure because included evidence was not quality-appraised, links from claims to individual evidence are often narrative, and counts and search windows are internally inconsistent.

citations.quote: This comprehensive review analyzes 126 studies published between 2011 and 2023 to examine current MBSE practices and their enablers (method, tool, and language) to identify the best strategies of application.

This paper presents a literature review on MBSE applications for space SE, aiming to synthesize best practices and identify strategic patterns that support standardized adoption across diverse mission contexts.

The comprehensive literature review (CLR) was conducted using the PRISMA guidelines as reference for a review procedure [34]. This investigation focuses exclusively on the application of MBSE within domain of space system engineering. It includes a wide range of studies covering various mission types from CubeSats to complex crewed missions.
These research questions (RQ) investigate how MBSE methods, modeling languages, and tools are implemented in space system engineering, structured around five defined MBSE phases.

RQ1: How have MBSE methodologies and their capabilities evolved? This question investigates the range of MBSE methods applied in space engineering and examines implementation patterns across the literature.

RQ2: What MBSE modeling languages and syntax are employed and what roles do they play across the SE lifecycle? This question identifies the languages and syntax used in MBSE application and examines their roles in supporting specific SE tasks.
RQ3: What tools are used to support MBSE implementation? This RQ retrieves MBSE tools referenced in the literature, analyzing their frequency utilization, and mapping their capabilities.

RQ4: What are the relationship between the MBSE phases and enablers? This question investigates how combinations of MBSE enablers contribute to achieving targeted SE objective and clarifies the realization of MBSE phases across the system lifecycle.

RQ5: What challenges are identified in the literature and how does the proposed method address them to improve MBSE application in space systems? This question explores the technical and methodological challenges observed in current practices and assesses how the proposed method offers opportunities for improved MBSE adoption and future research directions.
The databases of selected literature are Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science (WoS).
As of December 31, 2022, this search extracted 170 articles.
A Scopus search in February 2023 resulted in 191 articles extracted from conferences, proceedings, and journal articles.

A total of 24 reports are incorporated, comprising gray literature from MB4SE conference collections, ASCEND conferences, and NASA technical documents. Finally, the collection of all studies was consolidated into Mendeley and Zotero libraries. These tools managed references, removed duplicates, and filtered the initial pool of 386 articles from the general database.

The application of inclusion and exclusion criteria was carried out based on title, publication year, keywords, and search exclusions. The rest of selection criteria required a detailed review of the study content.
The research must contain space mission applications using MBSE.
Inclusive of all types and sizes of space missions (subsystems and space segment development, and existing missions).
All studies published before 2011 are omitted; this was applied during the database search.

Antenna deployment, embedded system, and software development applications through MBSE are excluded, despite their development for space, as this study focuses on the core subsystems of the space segment.

Initially, each study was mapped to one or more of the five MBSE phases to determine primary focus of the application, as summarized in Table 1. Then, the research questions RQ1, RQ2, and RQ3 were addressed by extracting and performing a quantitative analysis of the modeling languages, methods, and tools used in each study.

For RQ4, a qualitative analysis was conducted to examine relationship MBSE phases and enablers across the overall system lifecycle, as described Section 2.1. RQ5 explored challenges and opportunities through qualitative synthesis and cross analysis derived from the prior RQs. In addition, supplementary statistical data such as publication year, country, affiliation, journal type, and publisher were also analyzed.

Inter-rater reliability assessment was conducted to validate the consistency and reliability of article classification. The synthesis was carried out using Excel and full synthesis tables are provided in Appendices B-E.
The validity of the study is evaluated by three external reviewers, who possess expertise in MBSE, the space industry, and academia, to avoid default agreement between the authors.
The survey conducted covers 10% of the methods, all modeling languages and 20% of the tools from the total collected data rated by experts.
The assessment of reliability was used as feedback to identify and resolve classification ambiguity and to strengthen the credibility of the results.

citations.quote: Simulation and analysis are studied in 82 papers supporting architecture definition, functional and behavioral analysis of the system through integrated system models and executable model. These studies discuss model-based V&V, trade analysis and optimization, risk assessment and mitigation, and design feasibility.

Given that numerous studies provide incomplete information on the languages used, the enumeration of languages and their respective distribution was derived from the tools employed within the MBSE applications.
This review identified 68 tools, frameworks, and libraries used in the implementation of MBSE across various lifecycle stages and their function.

A considerable amount of literature references the utilization of multiple tools, a majority of which are designed to perform singular functions. Yet, a limited number of studies acknowledge the effort required to adapt these tools to varying mission scales and synchronization methodologies.
The exploration of lightweight and scalable MBSE strategies that do not compromise potential benefits remains largely unexamined.

This study had a significant scope of coverage; however, it encountered several notable limitations. Access-restricted publications and the potential exclusion of relevant articles from databases outside primary sources and variant date search posed completeness of dataset.

Finally, the underlying gap identified is that only a few studies explicitly demonstrate how MBSE supports the mission objectives. This lack of a targeted objective and the limited interpretation of the MBSE application may be a root cause for dispersed efforts and a lack of measurable outcomes (RQ5).
The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

After applying the selection criteria, 126 articles and reports were selected for detailed review.

there is no clear convergence around a unified MBSE practice within space industry. This diversity of practices poses challenges establishing consistent evaluation criteria or shared framework for assessing MBSE effectiveness.

However, the role of MBSE in later lifecycle stages, particularly during testing, integration, and verification, has poor visibility in literature, as indicated by the limited number of publications adequately reporting MBSE adoption Phases C and D.

Enhanced MBSE-2 refers to methodologies built on the classical SE methods that target specific phases of the lifecycle in system development to improve the efficiency, flexibility, and reusability of model artifacts and modeling processes.
Additionally, ambiguity in the reported use of MBSE enablers, where methods, language, and tools were used interchangeably and loosely referred to as "MBSE," posed classification challenges.

In summary, the taxonomy of MBSE languages in Figure 11 overviews the right half groups using purpose of application into two categories: general-purpose modeling languages and domain-specific languages. The left half groups integration and automation-supporting languages categorized into two: programming languages and data syntax to enable executive models and seamless exchange of digital artifacts.
Included study types from all sources are reports, peer-reviewed journals, and conference papers
